I taught English for 4 years in South Korea and I've seen it all. The culture there is absolutely obsessed with education for the sake of education, because they equate education and success, never mind what job you may have to do in order to achieve that "success". Oh, and "success" in South Korea equals money. Lots of money equals lots of status. So when you don't get into the SKY schools (the top 3 schools, equivalent to the Ivy League), and you don't get into a good school outside Korea, you are a failure for the rest of your life, according to conventional wisdom. So you have kids doing interviews for kindergartens, going to school for 8 hours a day, then private school for several more hours, then studying and doing homework until they pass out. Kids that choose to have fun and be kids? They are quickly left behind and make up the under-class when they get older. Kids that do what their parents tell them and study really hard and get into that good school and graduate and get the job at the big company pushing a pencil so they can get a big paycheck and their parents can brag... they end up getting to that job without a clue as to why they're there or what they're doing. That, coupled with excruciatingly long hours due to inherent flaws in their work culture (can't leave until the boss does, and the boss won't leave because he/she will look like a slacker) leads to South Korea being the least productive country per hour of work of any developed country. Turns out all that "education" is just veneer on a pile of shit.

The real peak will be when students leave school maximally in debt, such that they die before it's payed off. Maybe that means a 20 year super degree, or just higher prices.

There are still people working as burger flippers or cleaners without a 4 year degree, so there is room left before peak.

There are status driven people in every field.

There are top athletes who are obsessed about legacy and status, there are top scientists who are obsessed about legacy and status, there are top CEOs who are obsessed about legacy and status.

To openly claim that all college admissions is about status based one one individual is a pretty big fallacy. In any "competitive" arenas in life, you will have people who are status seekers there. However, not only are there tons of people are really do carry the so called "monastic love of learning" in my experience, there are also other reasons such as generous financial aid and school culture that attracts people to these schools. I know personally the choice came down to whether to go to a top public school (UC Berkeley on Regents) while taking out 10k loans a year for living expenses, vs a free ride to their rival school.

Is there a status motivation in that? I won't deny it. But to claim that it's the sole reason is just plain oversimplification.

To openly claim that all college admissions is about status based one one individual is a pretty big fallacy.

Genius Girl serves as an illustration, not conclusive proof. The big problem with the college admissions status seeking is that it's parents putting their kids in a pressure cooker, with the kids having very little say in the matter. They could gain the same quality education at a "lesser" school, but the pressure for an Ivy League comes down to one thing: if the kids gain status, the parents do too by taking credit for their success. It's child beauty pageants writ large.

The quest for an Ivy League education is a pile of horse shit. What you get out of college is more related to what you put into it rather than the name brand of your college.

However that assumes that you want an education out of college rather than rich friends and a certain kind of social life.
